note.note:
Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
28-year-old woman with first-time, left occipital throbbing headache since yesterday; no red-flag features. Impression: likely primary headache (migraine without aura > tension-type); safety-net provided.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Left-sided posterior head pain, throbbing, intensity 8/10, began mid-morning yesterday, gradual build-up, persistent.  
• Associated symptoms: Denies nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, visual aura, focal weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, neck stiffness, fever, chills, rash. Normal appetite, hydration, sleep.  
• Provocative/relieving factors: No change with position; minimal relief from single dose ibuprofen.  
• Pertinent negatives: No prior similar headaches; no recent trauma; no sinus or respiratory symptoms.  
• Past medical history: None reported.  
• Medications: None regularly; single dose ibuprofen yesterday.  
• Allergies: None reported.  
• Family history: Mother—hypertension, migraines.  
• Social / preventive: Lives with partner; designer (desk job); non-smoker; no alcohol or recreational drugs; no recent stressors identified.

Examination:
• Telehealth visit—no vitals recorded.  
• Patient oriented and conversational; no visual, speech, or motor deficits reported.  
• No neck stiffness or rash reported.  
• No physical examination performed.

Impression:
• Most likely: Migraine without aura – unilateral throbbing severe pain, functional impairment, positive family history, absence of secondary red-flags.  
• Alternative considerations:  
  – Tension-type headache – persistent ache without neurologic signs, but unilateral location and severity less typical.  
  – Cervicogenic headache – unilateral occipital location; sedentary work may contribute, though no neck pain or positional trigger.  
• Serious secondary causes (e.g., subarachnoid hemorrhage, intracranial mass) considered low likelihood given gradual onset, normal review of systems, and lack of neurologic findings; advised to monitor for red-flag evolution.

Plan:
• Pharmacologic: Prescribed stronger NSAID (specific agent not stated) to be taken regularly with food; may combine with acetaminophen as needed.  
• Supportive: Rest, adequate hydration.  
• Safety-net: Seek immediate review if pain worsens, persists beyond 1–2 days despite medication, or if new symptoms arise (fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness, visual changes, focal weakness).  
• Follow-up: Contact clinic in 1–2 days if no improvement; earlier if any red-flags develop.

Quality checks:

● Missing elements: Objective vitals, neurological exam, blood pressure measurement, full drug/allergy list confirmation, exact name/dose of prescribed NSAID, explicit follow-up appointment date.  
● Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality: Clear, minor pauses; lacked physical exam and precise medication details.
